name: soft-key-goal
task: Grab the key, and after that get to the goal square if you can.

value.feedback: CHANGES REQUIRED: the task commands getting to the goal square, but the only goal-making clause is the soft Existence(at_goal), which forces nothing, so FINAL_STATES is empty and the machine pays no reward for completing the task. The imperative 'get to the goal square if you can' does word reaching the goal as a preference, but then the preference cue covers that whole phrase: the hard Precedence(has_key, at_goal) plus the separate soft Existence(at_goal) splits one sentence into two unrelated clauses. Either way, if reaching the goal is only preferred, the task is preference-only and valid, but then the ordering 'after that' should be a hard Precedence(has_key, at_goal) with a soft Existence(at_goal) — which is exactly what was given. The real defect: if the intended reading is that reaching the goal is required (the sentence is an imperative command with an order), then Existence(at_goal) must be hard, which also forces has_key through the Precedence, making the whole task with a FINAL_STATE. If it is truly preferred, accept as given. Given the environment objective states the task is complete when the agent reaches the goal after using the key, the goal must be required: make Existence(at_goal) hard.

NO CHANGES NEEDED: the hard Existence(at_goal) requires reaching the goal, and the hard Precedence(has_key, at_goal) forbids it before the key is grabbed; together they force picking up the key first. The 'if you can' phrasing does not soften the imperative to reach the goal.

texts: Grab the key, and after that get to the goal square.
machine:
REWARD_MACHINE:
STATES: u0, u1, u2, u3
INITIAL_STATE: u0
FINAL_STATES: u3
REJECTING_STATES: u2
DEFAULT_REWARD: 0
TRANSITION_FUNCTION:
(u0, !at_goal&has_key) -> u1
(u0, at_goal&!has_key) -> u2
(u0, at_goal&has_key) -> u3
(u1, at_goal) -> u3
REWARD_FUNCTION:
(u0, at_goal&!has_key, u2) -> -10
(u0, at_goal&has_key, u3) -> 11
(u1, at_goal, u3) -> 11
